transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start off, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

I came in because... well, my sleep is just all broken up lately. I work overnight shifts as a personal care aide, and usually I can sleep during the day, but now I just lie there wide awake. And when I finally do drift off, I wake up feeling scared. It's like I never even rested at all.
Does this trouble sleeping happen only around your overnight work shifts, or do you also have trouble sleeping on your days off?

It's pretty much all the time now. Even on my days off. Like I was saying, I'll get off an overnight shift and just lie there wide awake, but it happens when I'm not working, too. My sleep is just completely broken up no matter what day it is. And then, yeah, when I do finally drift off, I just wake up scared... and I feel like I never rested at all.
When you wake up feeling scared, do you remember having a specific frightening dream or nightmare, or does the fear just come on without any dream you can recall?
I don't really remember any dreams. I just... I wake up and my heart is pounding, and I feel this awful sense of dread. But there's no specific nightmare I can point to. It's just the fear.
Have you ever experienced a traumatic or life-threatening event, such as an assault, accident, or something similarly frightening, at any point in your life?
No, I haven't. I mean, nothing like that. No accidents or assaults or anything. It's just... I just wake up feeling that way, but it's not because of something that happened to me in the past.
Aside from these nighttime awakenings, do you find yourself worrying excessively or feeling anxious during the day, even when you're not trying to sleep?

No, not really. I mean, I feel down and exhausted during the day, but I wouldn't call it worrying or feeling anxious. It's more just... feeling heavy and tired. The fear really only hits me when I wake up like that.
When these frightening awakenings happen, do they tend to occur shortly after you first fall asleep, or can they happen at any point during your sleep period?

It's hard to tell exactly when, because my sleep is just all broken up now. I'll get off my overnight shift and just... lie there wide awake for a long time. Then when I finally do manage to drift off, that's when I wake up scared. It just ruins whatever sleep I do get, and I always wake up feeling like I never rested at all.
Has anyone else who’s around when you wake up like this—like a roommate or family member—ever told you that you seemed to scream, thrash around, or appear confused before you were fully awake?

No, nobody's ever told me that. I mean, I'm usually by myself when I'm trying to sleep during the day anyway because of my shifts. But no, I don't think I scream or thrash around... at least, no one has ever said I do.
How long has this pattern of broken sleep and waking up scared been going on—days, weeks, or months?

It's been... well, definitely months. Actually, I think it's been about a year and two months now. It started right around the time my agency changed me over to rotating overnight shifts, and they started giving me all this extra paperwork to do.
On your days off, what time of day do you actually try to sleep—do you aim for nighttime sleep, or do you still sleep during the day like after a night shift?

I try to sleep at night on my days off. I mean, I want to be on a normal schedule when I'm not working. But... my body is just so confused from the rotating shifts that I don't really have a set time anymore. I just try to lay down whenever I feel too exhausted to keep my eyes open. So sometimes that's at night, but a lot of times it ends up being right in the middle of the day.
If you have several days off in a row with no work shifts at all, does your sleep eventually settle into a normal, restful pattern, or does it stay just as broken up as usual?

No, it stays just as broken up. Honestly, that's the main reason I came in to get help. My sleep is just all broken up now, no matter what. I can get off an overnight shift, or have a few days off, and I still just lie in bed wide awake. And then when I finally do manage to drift off, I just wake up scared... and I feel like I never rested at all.
When you do finally fall asleep, does the scary awakening usually happen soon after—within the first hour or so—or does it tend to happen later, closer to when you'd normally be waking up?

It's usually pretty soon after. Like I was just saying, it's all so broken up... I'll lie there wide awake for what feels like forever, and when I finally do manage to drift off, it feels like it's only an hour or so before I wake up scared again. It's never a full stretch of sleep. I never make it anywhere close to when I'm actually supposed to wake up, which is why I just always feel like I haven't rested at all.
When you wake up feeling scared, are you immediately clear-headed and aware of your surroundings, or do you feel confused and disoriented for a bit before you fully come to?

I'm pretty clear-headed right away, honestly. It's just... I wake up with this awful, scared feeling. Like I said before, that's really why I came in to get help, because my sleep is just completely broken up. I'll get off a shift, lie there wide awake for hours, and then when I finally do fall asleep, I just wake up terrified shortly after. I'm awake, I know where I am, but I'm just scared, and I feel like I haven't rested a single bit.
Did you already have episodes of waking up suddenly feeling scared like this before your schedule switched to rotating overnight shifts, or did that fear only start after the schedule change?

No, it didn't happen before the schedule change. This has been going on for about a year and two months now... ever since my agency switched me over to rotating overnight shifts and added on extra paperwork. That's when all this started.

latest_inference.note: The patient confirmed these fear awakenings began only after the shift to rotating overnight schedules and did not occur before, strongly supporting a circadian rhythm sleep disorder (shift work type). Lack of dream recall, no trauma history, no confusion/disorientation on waking, and no daytime worry argue against nightmare disorder, PTSD-related sleep disturbance, or sleep terror. This narrows the differential to shift work disorder rather than general unspecified insomnia.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports chronic (14-month) sleep disruption with insomnia and non-restorative sleep directly tied temporally to onset of rotating overnight shift work, persisting even on days off, indicating circadian misalignment consistent with Shift Work Disorder. The associated abrupt awakenings with fear/dread lack recalled nightmare content, dream mentation, confusion, or motor activity (no thrashing/screaming reported by others), and clear-headedness upon waking argues against Nightmare Disorder (F51.5) and Sleep Terror/NREM Parasomnia (G47.53). No trauma history rules out PTSD-related nightmares. No pervasive daytime anxiety/worry argues against a primary anxiety disorder. The temporal correlation with shift change, chronicity, and persistence despite days off supports circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder, shift work type.

confirmed_symptoms: Difficulty initiating sleep after overnight shifts
Sleep disruption persists even on days off
Non-restorative sleep despite lying down to sleep
Sleep pattern does not normalize even after several consecutive days off
Onset of symptoms coincided with switch to rotating overnight shift schedule
Wakes up with sudden fear/dread and pounding heart
No recalled nightmare or dream content
Clear-headed and oriented immediately upon waking (no confusion)
No reported screaming, thrashing, or confusion witnessed by others
Awakenings occur shortly after falling asleep, not late in sleep period

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Symptoms ongoing for approximately 14 months, beginning with transition to rotating overnight shift work.
additional_requirements: No history of trauma or life-threatening event reported, ruling out PTSD-related sleep disturbance
No significant daytime worry or anxiety reported, arguing against primary anxiety disorder
Symptoms did not predate schedule change, supporting causal link to shift work
No dream recall or nightmare content, arguing against Nightmare Disorder
No confusion or motor behavior during awakenings, arguing against NREM sleep arousal disorder (sleep terrors)
